title: The Balance Sheet Equation
context: Analyze how the balance sheet equation requires total assets to equal the sum of total liabilities and total equity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A pallet loader used by an operating business is classified as inventory because inventory can include any physical equipment a business owns.
A pallet loader held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as a non-current asset because the dealer is a business rather than a household.
A pallet loader kept in service by an operating business for more than one year is classified as a non-current tangible asset.
The same pallet loader must always be classified identically on every balance sheet regardless of how it is held.
The same pallet loader may be a non-current asset for one business and inventory for another, depending on whether it is used or held for sale.
tactical_explanations:
Physical form alone does not make a pallet loader inventory. Inventory is held for sale or for cycle consumption, not every machine the firm owns. Operating use beyond a year puts pallet loader among non-current tangibles. Counterexample: a forklift in the firm’s own warehouse is plant, not stock. Use-versus-resale is the split that matters.

So the statement is False.

A dealer’s pallet loader held for customers is merchandise. Resale intent keeps it in inventory (current), even though the dealer is a firm. A resale reading of the extract breaks this claim.

So the statement is False.

Multi-year operating use of a pallet loader fits the non-current tangible test. Useful life beyond the period plus own use, not resale, drive that line. Tangible means physical substance; non-current means long-term benefit. Operators and dealers can report the same pallet loader on different lines. Short-term claims belong with current liabilities; long-dated borrowings stay non-current. Period profit flows to retained earnings; it is not a separate cash-flow line. Customer collections recycle earlier sales through operating cash. Plant bought for cash is an investing outflow, not day-to-day operating spend.

So the statement is True.

The same pallet loader need not share one balance-sheet line everywhere. Each reporter classifies by how it holds the object. Operator → non-current tangible; dealer → inventory. Physical identity does not freeze the category. How pallet loader is held and for how long decides the balance-sheet line. Settlement timing and intended use matter more than physical shape for pallet loader. Operators and dealers can report the same pallet loader on different lines. Customer collections recycle earlier sales through operating cash.

So the statement is False.

Intended use decides the line for the same physical object. An operator records a non-current tangible; a dealer records inventory. A dealer’s pallet loader stays inventory until sold.

So the statement is True.

title: Assets Equal Liabilities Plus Equity
context: Review how owner's equity is derived as the residual claim remaining once liabilities are deducted from assets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Classifying a pallet loader as a non-current asset depends mainly on its purchase price rather than on management's intended use.
Classifying a pallet loader as a non-current asset depends on management's intention to use it in operations rather than to sell it quickly.
A pallet loader acquired for resale still counts among non-current assets as long as it remains unsold for several months.
A pallet loader used daily in a business's own operations should be recorded as inventory because it wears out over time.
Once a dealer sells a pallet loader from its stock, the buyer must continue to record it as inventory.
tactical_explanations:
Purchase price measures cost; it does not choose inventory vs fixed asset. Management intent, operate or resell, decides the class. A cheap pallet loader used for years is still non-current; a costly one held for sale is inventory. Balance-sheet lines are read from the reporter’s purpose, not from generic labels. A loader reading of the extract breaks this claim. Operators and dealers can report the same pallet loader on different lines. Short-term claims belong with current liabilities; long-dated borrowings stay non-current. Period profit flows to retained earnings; it is not a separate cash-flow line.

So the statement is False.

Intent to use the asset in operations beyond one period places it among non-current assets. Resale intent would have put the same object in inventory.

So the statement is True.

Goods bought for resale enter inventory immediately. Sitting unsold for months does not promote them into non-current assets. Resale intent, not shelf time, decides the line. Short-term claims belong with current liabilities; long-dated borrowings stay non-current. Period profit flows to retained earnings; it is not a separate cash-flow line.

So the statement is False.

Wear is handled by depreciating a fixed asset, not by calling operating kit inventory. Daily own use of a pallet loader supports non-current classification. Counterexample: factory machines wear out yet sit in plant & equipment. Plant bought for cash is an investing outflow, not day-to-day operating spend. Residual value reduces the depreciable base before the annual charge is calculated. A dealer’s pallet loader stays inventory until sold. Own use of a pallet loader for years makes it a tangible fixed asset. Year 1 and Year 2 columns give the pair of totals needed for the percentage.

So the statement is False.

After the sale, the buyer’s purpose governs classification. If the buyer puts the machine into operations, it becomes the buyer’s non-current asset. Own use of a pallet loader for years makes it a tangible fixed asset.

So the statement is False.

NCL-to-equity share = non-current liabilities ÷ total equity.

$$
\text{NCL share} = \frac{\text{non-current liabilities}}{\text{total equity}}
$$

$$
\text{NCL} = 220 + 63
$$

$$
\text{NCL} = 283
$$

$$
\text{Equity} = 839
$$

$$
\frac{283}{839} \approx 0.3373
$$

$$
\approx 33.7\%
$$

33.7\% < 56.8\%

Year-2 NCL/equity is 33.7%, below the 56.8% claim.

So the statement is True.

Long-term financing surplus = (equity + non-current liabilities) ÷ non-current assets − 1.

$$
\text{Surplus} = \frac{\text{equity} + \text{NCL}}{\text{NCA}} - 1
$$

$$
\text{Equity} + \text{NCL} = 761 + 267
$$

$$
= 1{,}028
$$

$$
\text{NCA} = 740
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740}
$$

$$
\approx 1.3892
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740} - 1
$$

$$
\approx 0.3892
$$

$$
\approx 38.9\%
$$

38.9\% > 7.3\%

Year-2 NCL/equity is 38.9%, above the 7.3% claim.

So the statement is True.

Percentage growth for Total equity is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{Y_2 - Y_1}{Y_1}
$$

$$
Y_1 = 761, \quad Y_2 = 839
$$

$$
Y_2 - Y_1 = 839 - 761
$$

$$
= 78
$$

$$
\frac{78}{761} \approx 0.1025
$$

$$
\approx 10.2\%

= 98

$$
\frac{98}{1{,}181}
$$

$$

$$
\approx 8.3\%
